diagnosis.what_is_wrong: The trace does not establish an infrastructure fault explaining the slower coding task. It does show a workload shift to sustained python3 execution in the only observed container, but aggregate CPU use stayed modest and the scheduler samples show CPUs idle before switching to python3; this is consistent with work being done, not host CPU saturation or demonstrated scheduling delay.
diagnosis.root_cause_service: python3 in pid_ns 4026531836 (observed workload; not established as a fault source)
diagnosis.evidence: Compared full-span CPU/runtime windows using the workers' run_python analysis: python3 rises from 23.9 ms in 03:27:30.200–03:27:38.200 to 1,922.8 ms in 03:27:46.200–03:27:54.200, then is still elevated at 754.2 ms in 03:27:54.200–03:28:02.100. However total CPU was about 2.018 core-seconds over the 8-second high-python range on a four-CPU host, not evidence of host saturation. Raw scheduler lines around 03:27:48–03:27:52 show python3 switched in from swapper/idle, and the workers' wakeup pairing did not establish a competing runnable queue. Adjacent 10-second ranges also show block issue/complete counts matching (377/378, 149/149, 43/43) and modest network counts with successful rc=0 transmissions. ctf_timeline returned no matches for the requested common names, so the workers used the trace DataFrame’s event index/rates instead; ctf_lines failed, and indexed raw records were inspected. The falsifying check for CPU contention—whether python3 was held off-CPU behind runnable work—was run and was not supported by the sampled switch context.
diagnosis.window_evidence: The candidate window comes from the per-process sched_stat_runtime change: python3 is negligible through 03:27:38.200, increases through the transition, is near 0.96 CPU-seconds in each 4-second interval from 03:27:46.200 to 03:27:54.200, and remains elevated through the 03:27:54.200–03:27:58.200 slice. It drops sharply in the 03:27:58.200–03:28:00.200 2-second bin. This bounds the observed workload burst, not a proven incident.
